title: AlphaNIST — supplementary film
voice: Stock synthetic English narration; no voice cloning
scope: Simulation footage. Selected successful runs are illustrations, not a success-rate evaluation. Single-component and ten-component policies are different trained models.

sections.title: Ten components, one episode
sections.visual: Continuous fixed-view ten-component episode with synchronized close-up. Keep real-time motion; identify the long reach without cutting away.
sections.narration: Watch this ten-component assembly, without cuts. The robot must assemble every active component, but the task does not prescribe an order. Notice the long reach across the board, and the small contacts used to turn the nut.
sections.evidence: Selected successful ten-component rollout; Method and Experiments, multi-component setting.

sections.title: An outcome, not a sequence of instructions
sections.visual: Continue the same episode and both synchronized views. Do not speed up or change the chronology.
sections.narration: There is no separate planner choosing a sequence of skills. These actions come from one learned policy. The task reward arrives only when all ten assemblies are complete, not after each intermediate step.
sections.evidence: Experiments: Emergent Strategies over Long Horizons.

sections.title: The question behind the behavior
sections.visual: Finish the same uninterrupted episode. Label long-range manipulation, then leave completion visible.
sections.narration: If success is so far away, where does useful experience come from? Alpha NIST combines diverse starting states, shared training across assemblies, and large-scale simulation.
sections.evidence: Method: Reset Coverage and Experience Allocation; Shared Policy and Robot Control.

sections.title: The assembly problem
sections.visual: An assembled-board asset overview, followed by a cluttered ten-component episode excerpt. The overview is an asset illustration, not policy execution. Name object displacement descriptively.
sections.narration: The NIST board brings together twenty assemblies, with parts as small as four millimeters. A grasp that lifts a part may still block its insertion. With several parts present, the robot must also work around clutter and neighboring assemblies.
sections.evidence: Introduction; Experiments: short- and long-horizon strategies.

sections.title: Reward the outcome
sections.visual: Simple outcome diagram: reach, grasp and partial insertion receive no assembly-progress reward; complete assembly receives the task reward. Explicit small note for control costs.
sections.narration: We use a binary task reward for completed assembly. Reaching, grasping, and partial insertion receive no assembly-progress reward. Separate control costs discourage large actions, rapid motion, and excessive torque. The objective specifies the result, not a rewarded sequence of maneuvers.
sections.evidence: Method: Binary Full-Assembly Objective, including per-step control regularization.

sections.title: Make useful experience available
sections.visual: Existing reset showcase. Label it as sampled starting states, not robot actions. Include loose, held and partially assembled examples.
sections.narration: A binary objective does not mean always starting from loose parts. A cached bank provides valid states, from objects on the table to in-hand grasps and partial assemblies. These are starting conditions, not demonstrations or prescribed stages. The policy must still discover how to finish.
sections.evidence: Method: Reset Coverage and Experience Allocation; reset-only showcase contains no policy actions.

sections.title: Spend experience near the learning frontier
sections.visual: Illustrative beta-sampling curve versus recent reset success: nonzero at both endpoints, largest near intermediate success. Mark the graphic as a sampling rule, not measured data.
sections.narration: Which states should the learner revisit? Success-guided sampling favors intermediate recent success: neither almost always solved, nor almost always failed. Every cached state retains some chance of being sampled. This choice spans the entire assembly-and-reset bank, selecting both the geometry and the starting condition.
sections.evidence: Method beta-sampling equation: probability proportional to epsilon plus square root of p times one minus p, normalized over the joint bank.

sections.title: Share the learner across geometries
sections.visual: Restrained input-to-policy-to-control diagram, with geometry, robot state and action history. Show different assembly examples as context, not separate policy heads.
sections.narration: For single-component experiments, one policy trains across all twenty tasks using P P O. It observes robot state and surface point clouds, without a discrete task label. Different geometries share the same learner and completion objective.
sections.evidence: Method: Shared Policy and Robot Control. The diagram describes the single-component policy, not a claimed identical k10 architecture.

sections.title: Does sharing help?
sections.visual: Two bars: 98.2% shared binary-task-reward policy and 81.4% mean of twenty separate binary-task-reward policies. Persistent labels: mixed-reset training success; 64K environments per run; 25K iterations; budgets matched per run, not total compute.
sections.narration: Does sharing help? With binary task rewards, the shared policy reaches ninety-eight point two percent training success, versus eighty-one point four averaged over twenty separate policies. These results include partially assembled starts, with budgets matched per run. The tested dense reward does not show the same benefit from sharing.
sections.evidence: Experiments: Asset Heterogeneity Enables Learning. 98.2 and 81.4 are training success, not random-start evaluation.

sections.title: Scale and sampling both matter
sections.visual: Evaluation plot with 1K:38.6, 4K:78.9, 8K:86.9, 256K:97.4, plus uniform-reset training baseline at 256K:84.3. Label log environment axis and evaluation protocol. No invented error bars.
sections.narration: In a separate evaluation, success improves with parallel experience. At two hundred and fifty-six thousand environments, success-guided sampling reaches ninety-seven point four percent, versus eighty-four point three with uniform sampling. Both use a common mixed-reset evaluation bank. Scale and the allocation of experience matter together.
sections.evidence: Experiments: Sparse Binary Task Rewards Amplify Scaling Gains; five evaluation seeds, 32 trials per asset per seed, stochastic actions, 15-second episodes, 25K-iteration checkpoints.

sections.title: Grasp adaptation
sections.visual: 8 mm peg: center grasp, release, end regrasp, insertion. First show the motion slowly, then replay or hold its five-frame sequence. Label any slowed footage and replay.
sections.narration: Look at what completion can require. This peg is held near its center: a successful pickup, but an inconvenient grasp for insertion. The gripper releases it and regrasps near one end, exposing more shaft. We call this grasp adaptation. No grasp-changing instruction was supplied.
sections.evidence: Experiments: Emergent Strategies over Short Horizons; visually checked peg clip and gallery sequence.

sections.title: Board-assisted reorientation
sections.visual: Waterproof connector: board contact changes pose, followed by lift and insertion. Slow the short maneuver with an explicit speed label; show a replay or the corresponding sequence.
sections.narration: For this connector, the board becomes part of the manipulation. Surface contact changes the part's orientation before insertion: board-assisted reorientation. The useful motion is not confined to what the fingers can do while holding the object in free space.
sections.evidence: Experiments: extrinsic reorientation; visually checked waterproof connector clip.

sections.title: Contact-driven threading
sections.visual: M4 one-sided fingertip tapping, followed by M16 circular fingertip contacts. Label separate assemblies and slowed motion. Do not imply they are one continuous rollout or the same checkpoint.
sections.narration: Threading shows another kind of contact-driven motion. On the small nut, repeated one-sided contacts advance the thread. On the larger nut, the fingers move around it through successive contacts. We call these fingertip tapping and circular threading: different solutions, not instructions written into the task.
sections.evidence: Short-horizon strategy section and qualitative gallery. M4 is a saved-state replay from an earlier trained policy; examples span checkpoints.

sections.title: Object separation and assembly
sections.visual: A second complete ten-component episode, 28.26 seconds at real time. Wide plus synchronized detail. Label overlapping-gear displacement around 4–8 seconds as object separation, not asserted intent.
sections.narration: Return to a cluttered board. Overlapping parts are displaced, and a gear is then picked up and assembled. Object separation names the visible behavior, without assuming human-like reasoning about obstacles. This is a separately trained ten-component policy. We leave the successful episode running so the local motions can be seen in the context of the whole task.
sections.evidence: Selected complete ten-component rollout; qualitative evidence only. K1 and K10 are different trained policies.

sections.title: What this establishes—and what remains open
sections.visual: Hold the completed final board, then a minimal scope card. Keep the end frame uncluttered. No new synthetic robot imagery.
sections.narration: All results are in simulation. Physical transfer and continuous twenty-component assembly under one terminal objective remain open. What we see here is that diverse starts and shared experience can support several kinds of dexterous behavior under a common completion objective.
sections.evidence: Limitations and Conclusion. Selected successful demonstrations are not a success-rate estimate.
